paragraphs.text: Servián-Morilla et al. (2016) studied a consanguineous family from southern Spain with 17 members across 3 generations. Four of 5 sibs in generation II had limb-girdle muscular dystrophy, with weakness mainly in the proximal lower limbs and onset in the third decade. The disease progressed, leading to scapular winging and wheelchair confinement. Serum creatine kinase was normal in 3 patients and mildly elevated in 1. Muscle biopsies from all 4 affected sibs ranged from very mild myopathic changes to classic dystrophic pathology. Of the proteins typically affected in myopathies, only alpha-dystroglycan was reduced. Leg muscle MRI showed early fatty replacement of the internal regions of the thigh muscles, sparing the external areas. This 'from inside-to-outside' degeneration progressed over the years and did not match patterns seen in other muscular dystrophies. Transmission electron microscopy showed normal muscle ultrastructure and normal basement membrane compaction. The patients had no skin abnormalities.

paragraphs.text: Servián-Morilla et al. (2020) reported 15 patients from 9 unrelated families, including the original family. The families came from Spain, Bulgaria, Italy, Germany, the USA, Iran, and the United Arab Emirates, and 4 of the 9 families were consanguineous. One patient had a congenital presentation, 2 had infantile onset before 3 years of age, and 12 had adult onset. Of the adult-onset patients, 58.3% began in the second decade, 25% in the third, and 16.6% in the fourth to fifth decades. Weakness was proximal, clearly predominant in the lower limbs, and slowly progressive. Seven patients (46.6%) with onset in their teens used a wheelchair between the third and fifth decades. Mild to moderate scapular winging was present in 11 of the 15 patients. The congenital case presented with hypotonia and proximal lower limb weakness after gait acquisition. He later developed mild weakness, wasting, and contractures of the upper limbs, with mild facial weakness, ptosis, and nasal voice. Six patients had mild to severe respiratory involvement from the mid-forties onward, and 2 of them needed nighttime ventilatory support. No significant bulbar, cardiac, or other systemic manifestations were found. In the text, serum CK was normal except in 4 patients with mild elevation (2 to 6 times normal). However, the clinical table listed elevated CK in more patients, up to 10 times normal. The table also noted a patient with infantile onset (family 9) who had nystagmus and retinitis pigmentosa. For 2 of the 4 originally reported sibs, the table gave onset in the second decade.

paragraphs.text: Muscle MRI or CT of the lower limbs was available for 11 of the 15 patients reported by Servián-Morilla et al. The pattern specifically involved the vastus lateralis, medialis, and intermedius, the posterior thigh compartment, and the gastrocnemius. It was clearest in early disease but could still be seen in the vastus lateralis at end stage. The lower leg muscles were better preserved than the thigh muscles. Biopsies from the vastus lateralis were dystrophic. Biopsies from the biceps brachii showed mild myopathic features, with lobulated fibers in some cases.

paragraphs.text: Servián-Morilla et al. (2016) performed whole-exome sequencing in 2 affected sibs and their healthy sister from the consanguineous Spanish family. In the POGLUT1 gene they found a homozygous c.699T-G transversion, resulting in an asp233-to-glu (D233E) substitution, and the variant segregated with the disease. It was absent from the ExAC database (60,698 individuals) and from 919 DNA samples from 57 populations. The mutation did not affect POGLUT1 expression in muscle or its localization in the endoplasmic reticulum. The purified mutant enzyme had much lower O-glucosyltransferase activity than wildtype toward an EGF repeat from human factor IX and toward 5 EGF repeats from mouse Notch1. It also had lower O-xylosyltransferase activity but kept some residual enzymatic activity. In Drosophila lacking Rumi (the fly POGLUT1) enzymatic activity, wildtype human POGLUT1 rescued the muscle defects, whereas the D233E mutant gave only weak and variable rescue.

paragraphs.text: Servián-Morilla et al. (2020) studied 15 patients with LGMDR21 from 9 families. Sequencing used gene panels or whole-exome sequencing, and all variants were confirmed by Sanger sequencing. Across the cohort they identified 9 missense variants and 1 nonsense variant in POGLUT1, in homozygous or compound heterozygous state. Homozygous missense variants were found in patients from 6 families: I129T, R98W, Y57C, W308L, and C102F (all novel), and R183W, previously described as a Dowling-Degos disease mutation. Two affected sibs in family 8 were compound heterozygous for Y156N and a c.552G-A transition that creates a stop codon (W184X). In public databases, the novel variants were either absent or seen in the heterozygous state in 1 or 2 individuals out of more than 60,000 controls.

paragraphs.text: Servián-Morilla et al. (2020) tested the variants functionally. In HEK293T cells, the R183W and Y57C mutants were secreted normally, but the purified proteins had much lower O-glucosyltransferase activity than wildtype. In the Drosophila rumi myogenesis rescue assay, R183W, I129T, and Y57C gave partial rescue, similar to D233E, and C102F gave no rescue. Y156N was not tested. The authors predicted that W184X would be inactive because it removes the substrate-binding site.

paragraphs.text: Servián-Morilla et al. (2016) studied muscle from patients homozygous for the D233E mutation. Compared with controls, it showed reduced NOTCH1 intracellular domain, lower HES1 and PAX7 mRNA levels, and fewer PAX7-positive satellite cells. These changes were not found in age-matched patients with other muscular dystrophies or with secondary dystroglycanopathies. Patient muscle showed reduced glycosylation of alpha-dystroglycan and reduced laminin binding, but agrin binding was normal. In patient skin fibroblasts, alpha-dystroglycan glycosylation and laminin binding were normal. Primary myoblasts from patients proliferated slowly, had fewer self-renewing PAX7-positive cells, and differentiated more readily. Overexpressing the NOTCH1 intracellular domain in immortalized patient myoblasts reversed the proliferation defect and the facilitated differentiation, but did not restore the number of PAX7-positive cells. Blocking Notch signaling in differentiating C2C12 cells reduced glycosylated alpha-dystroglycan. The authors concluded that loss of satellite cells due to reduced Notch signaling was a key disease mechanism. They proposed that the alpha-dystroglycan hypoglycosylation was secondary.

agent.process_note: Read the full texts of Servián-Morilla et al. (2016) and Servián-Morilla et al. (2020). Straub et al. (2018) was available as a title only, so I cited it only for the existence of the ENMC nomenclature workshop. Checked variant names, zygosity, family and patient counts, and the clinical table directly against the texts. The 2020 paper does not give nucleotide changes for most variants, nor the country of origin of each family; only the overall list of countries and the consanguinity count are given. The 2020 paper is internally inconsistent about the family 2 genotype (homozygous R279Q in the results text, compound heterozygous D233E/R279Q in the table and myoblast studies) and about CK elevation. Both discrepancies are described rather than resolved. The reference data did not supply a MIM number for POGLUT1, so none is given.
